source_refs.note: Topic 3.2, printed pages 49-51, as printed: history of cell theory, its three points, validation and exceptions, with Figure 3.1 where it is printed.

blocks.text: At the beginning of 17th century, many scientists began the use of microscopes to study very small objects. In 1665, English scientist Robert Hooke examined a thin slice of cork of oak tree under microscope. He observed that the cork was made of “many little boxes”. Hooke also examined the pieces of stem and root of oak tree under microscope. He found that these were also made of similar little boxes. He concluded that the parts of plants were made of compartments. Hooke named these compartments as “cellulae”.

blocks.alt: Drawing of Robert Hooke's microscope: a long tilted tube on a pillar above a round base, with a piece of cork held on a pin below the objective end. Beside it, a circular view of a thin slice of cork showing many small, closed, box-like cells sharing their walls.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.1: Robert Hooke's microscope and observation (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.1).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Piece of cork (on the specimen pin of the microscope); Little boxes in cork (the magnified slice).

blocks.text: In 1673, a Dutch scientist Anton van Leeuwenhoek made a better microscope and observed living cells in pond water. He called these cells as animalcules.

In 1809, the French biologist Jean Baptiste de-Lamarck also observed cells when he examined the parts of animals and plants under microscope. Later on, in 1831 the British botanist Robert Brown discovered nucleus in the cell.

After these studies, biologists began to organize information about cells. In 1838, the German botanist Matthias Schleiden observed many parts of plants under microscope. He concluded that all plants were composed of cells. The next year, the German zoologist Theodor Schwann concluded the same for animals. In 1885, the German physician Rudolf Virchow (1821–1902) observed that all cells come from other cells. In 1862, Louis Pasteur provided the experimental proof of this idea. These observations were combined to form a basic theory about cells. It is called cell theory. It has three essential points.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints 1885 for Virchow's observation, which cannot be right because Pasteur's proof of the same idea is dated 1862. Virchow stated that all cells come from other cells (omnis cellula e cellula) in 1855.

items: All living organisms are composed of one or more cells.
Cells are the basic units of structure and function in an organism.
Cells come only from the division of pre-existing cells.
